title: Instructional Design
description: Design learning experiences around goals, practice, and evidence.

questions.prompt: What should guide the choice of an instructional activity?
questions.explanation: Activities should give learners practice with the knowledge or skill specified in the learning goal.

questions.prompt: Learning objectives are more useful when they describe observable performances.
questions.explanation: Observable outcomes help align instruction and assessment; not every meaningful goal is reducible to a simple score.

questions.prompt: A lecture is ineffective for every learning objective.
questions.explanation: Direct explanation can efficiently introduce ideas, but learners also need appropriate practice and feedback.

questions.prompt: Which practices can reduce extraneous cognitive load?
questions.explanation: Reducing irrelevant demands and structuring information frees limited working-memory resources for learning.

questions.prompt: Prior knowledge can change how difficult new material feels.
questions.explanation: Existing schemas support integration but misconceptions can also interfere with new learning.

questions.prompt: A worked example is especially helpful when learners:
options: Are new to a complex procedure
questions.explanation: Worked examples reduce unguided search for novices; support can fade as expertise grows.

questions.prompt: Learners benefit from support that is adjusted as competence develops.
questions.explanation: Scaffolding should respond to current performance and gradually shift responsibility to learners.

questions.prompt: What is constructive alignment?
options: Matching outcomes, learning activities, and assessments
Using the same textbook in every course
Teaching only what is easiest to test
questions.explanation: Alignment makes practice and assessment reflect the intended learning outcomes.

questions.prompt: More content coverage always produces more learning.
questions.explanation: Overloading content can crowd out practice, feedback, and time for durable understanding.

questions.prompt: Which can make an explanation easier to follow?
options: Connect new ideas to relevant prior knowledge
Break a process into meaningful steps
Use a diagram when it clarifies structure
Add details unrelated to the learning goal
questions.explanation: Coherent sequencing and relevant representations support understanding; irrelevant detail adds load.

questions.prompt: An instructional scaffold should remain fixed regardless of learners’ progress.
questions.explanation: Support should be responsive; excessive help can become unnecessary as learners gain expertise.

questions.prompt: Why include examples and non-examples?
options: They remove the need for practice
questions.explanation: Contrasting examples can help learners identify defining and non-defining features.

questions.prompt: Transfer is more likely when learners practice applying knowledge in varied, relevant contexts.
questions.explanation: Variation can help learners recognize underlying principles beyond a single example.

questions.prompt: Which help make instruction accessible?
options: Provide captions or transcripts where appropriate
Offer more than one way to engage
Rely on color alone to convey meaning
questions.explanation: Multiple accessible representations and clear organization support learners with differing needs.

questions.prompt: A memorable activity is necessarily an effective learning activity.
questions.explanation: Engagement can support learning, but activity quality depends on alignment, practice, and resulting understanding.

questions.prompt: When should a teacher check for understanding?
options: Only at the end of the course
questions.explanation: Frequent low-stakes checks reveal misunderstandings while there is still time to respond.

questions.prompt: Retrieval practice can be incorporated as a low-stakes classroom activity.
questions.explanation: Brief recall prompts help learners strengthen memory and help instructors identify gaps.

questions.prompt: Which are signs of an aligned assessment?
questions.explanation: Assessments should measure the intended outcome with transparent criteria, not irrelevant advantages.

questions.prompt: A single instructional method is optimal for every learner and every topic.
questions.explanation: Effective design depends on goals, learners’ prior knowledge, content, and context.

questions.prompt: Designing a course includes planning how evidence will inform later revisions.
questions.explanation: Reviewing learner work and outcomes can reveal where instruction needs adjustment.
